faqs.q: When can bats be removed from a Columbia home?
faqs.a: Bat work here is exclusion only, and no permit is required to remove bats in South Carolina. What controls the timing is SCDNR guidance, which we follow: complete exclusions are planned for early spring (March-April) or fall (August-October), and we do not run a full exclusion from May through mid-July, sometimes into August, because flightless pups would be trapped inside. That window is agency guidance, not a state law. We can inspect and map every entry at any time of year, and a bat found inside your living space is different — keep the room closed and call us, because bats in living quarters are a rabies-testing situation handled with the Department of Public Health.

faqs.q: I saw a snake near my Columbia home. Should I be worried?
faqs.a: Most snakes our crew is called about here are harmless rat snakes, black racers, and garter snakes following rodents and frogs. The ones that change the call are the copperhead, which is statewide, and — only in the wet coastal and swamp country — the cottonmouth. We identify first, from a safe distance: keep kids and pets inside, do not try to move or kill it, and tell us where it went. The southern hognose snake of the Sandhills is State Threatened and is never handled as a removal job, and venomous snakes are safety-and-referral work, not a guaranteed capture.

Forest Acres keeps our crew busy around the Trenholm Road canopy suburbs and Satchel Ford creek corridors. Two problems account for most visits: bats behind shutters and in gable vents, and skunks denning under decks.

Postwar brick and frame homes, lake and river cottages, and newer subdivisions share the same streets, with pine canopy hanging over most roofs. Removal without repair does not hold in Forest Acres, so our visits pair the animal work with sealing and screening sized to the house itself.

faqs.q: We have rats in our Blythewood attic. How is that different from squirrels?

Blythewood.wildlife_intro:
Ask around Blythewood and the wildlife stories usually trace back to the Sandhills subdivisions and farm edges in the county's northeast. Homeowners here phone us first about armadillos in pine-straw beds and lawns, then about opossums in crawlspaces.

Older homes near the town center give way to ranch subdivisions and then to farmhouses on the outskirts, and the wildlife entries change with each ring. Pine straw is the Midlands detail that matters most: copperheads vanish into it, armadillos root through it, and raccoons cross it nightly from creek woods to rooftops.

Before we leave a Blythewood home, the roofline, foundation line, and any outbuilding we worked on get rechecked opening by opening — that recheck is what keeps one call from becoming three.

faqs.q: How do rats get into Eastover homes?
faqs.a: Around Eastover, rats follow food and cover: bird feeders, pet food, ivy and brush against the house, and the lines and limbs that reach the roof near Congaree floodplain farm country in the county's southeast. The job is trapping inside, sealing every entry we find, and cutting the routes and food that drew them. We will show you the droppings and rub marks we used to confirm the species, because rat work fails when it is guessed at.

faqs.q: There are bats in my Eastover attic. When can they be removed?
faqs.a: Bats are excluded, never trapped or killed, and South Carolina requires no permit to remove them. Timing follows SCDNR guidance rather than a state ban: complete exclusions are scheduled for early spring (March–April) or late summer into fall (August–October), because excluding in May through mid-July can trap flightless pups inside. In Eastover we fit one-way exits over the entry points used by colonies near Congaree floodplain farm country in the county's southeast, seal every other gap of 3/8 inch or more, and clean guano once the colony is out. A single bat found in living quarters is different — do not handle it, and it should go to the SC Department of Public Health for rabies testing.

faqs.q: What will the crew need to do at my Eastover house?

From there a Eastover job usually combines removing the animal — by one-way eviction or trapping under depredation rules — with sealing, screening, and any cleanup the animal left behind. Jobs near Congaree floodplain farm country in the county's southeast with older construction tend to need more sealing; newer homes often need less. The inspection report is what sets the scope, not a phone guess.

The pattern in Eastover is set by the Congaree floodplain farm country in the county's southeast. If we had to name this town's signature jobs, they would be gray squirrels in mature pine canopy and raccoons working creek corridors.

Brick ranches from the 1960s and 1970s, older in-town homes near the center, and fast-growing subdivisions at the edges give this housing stock three distinct generations of rooflines to inspect. River and lake country surrounds these neighborhoods — creeks, coves, and wooded drains run behind the subdivisions — giving raccoons, squirrels, and bats a covered route to almost every roofline.

Every job in Eastover ends the same way it should: openings found on the inspection closed in steel mesh and flashing, so the house near Congaree floodplain farm country in the county's southeast stops advertising vacancies to the next animal that passes.

faqs.q: Something is digging up my Hopkins lawn at night and it smells like skunk. What is going on?
faqs.a: That combination is a striped skunk hunting grubs — the small cone-shaped holes across a lawn are its signature — and a den under a porch, deck, or crawlspace edge is usually nearby. Skunks are South Carolina's number-two rabies carrier in Department of Public Health testing, and routine relocation is against state law, so our crew traps calmly at the den with covered traps, handles the animal under SCDNR depredation rules, and screens the den opening so the next skunk finds it closed.

faqs.q: Why do squirrels keep getting into Hopkins attics?
faqs.a: Gray squirrels need an opening little more than an inch wide, and the usual doors here are soffit corners, gable vents, and the gaps where additions meet the main roof, reached from fences and overhanging limbs. Trapping without sealing just invites the next squirrel, so our crew fits one-way doors, lets the animals leave, and seals every opening in steel — timed so a nursing litter is never sealed inside.
